title: Beyond Monolingual Assumptions: A Survey on Code-Switched NLP in the Era of Large Language Models across Modalities
problem_statement: How Large Language Models handle code-switched inputs across text, speech, and vision-language modalities, why multilingual pre-training fails to guarantee robust code-switching performance, and how existing architectural designs, dataset shortages, and evaluation biases restrict effective deployment in multilingual societies.
domain: Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Code-Switching and Code-Mixing, Multilingual Computing, Multimodal AI (Speech and Vision-Language Processing), Low-Resource Languages
theoretical_framework: Sociolinguistic and grammatical theories of code-switching (including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint model and structural switch-point constraints), quantitative code-mixing metrics (Code-Mixing Index [CMI], S-index, M-index, I-index, and SyM-CoM), cross-lingual representation alignment in foundation models, and multimodal fusion architectures.
methodology: Systematic literature review and taxonomic synthesis analyzing 327 studies across 15+ NLP tasks, 30+ datasets, and 80+ languages; categorizing research into pre-LLM versus LLM eras, five core research directions, training paradigms (pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning, PEFT, RLAIF), multimodal speech and vision applications, and evaluation methodologies to identify persistent failure modes and outline a future research roadmap.
key_findings: Multilingual pre-training alone does not ensure code-switching proficiency; large language models frequently underperform compared to smaller, task-specific fine-tuned models on code-switched inputs because pre-training corpora contain limited naturalistic code-switched data.

Large language models exhibit asymmetric transfer and language confusion; models process English tokens embedded within non-English contexts better than non-English tokens within English contexts, and standard fine-tuning amplifies unintended language generation.

Current code-switching research exhibits extreme resource concentration; over 72% of speech datasets and 92% of social media code-switching datasets involve English (predominantly Hindi-English, Spanish-English, and Mandarin-English), leaving non-English pairs, African languages, Southeast Asian languages, and trilingual settings critically underexplored.

Synthetic code-switching generation methods expand training volume but achieve only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to capture spontaneous conversational behavior, orthographic variations, transliteration nuances, and sociolinguistic pragmatic intent.

Standard evaluation metrics (such as BLEU, Word Error Rate, and perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators correlate poorly with human judgments on code-switched generation and speech tasks, overestimating model performance and failing to capture switch-point dynamics.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, curriculum-based instruction tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback improve low-resource adaptation, but speech and vision-language multimodal code-switching systems lag significantly behind text-based natural language understanding.
scope_and_delimitations: The survey synthesizes academic research on code-switched natural language processing, focusing primarily on large language models and foundation models while contextualizing historical methods from statistical and neural eras.
The review spans 15+ natural language processing tasks across token-level, sentence-level, generation, conversational, reasoning, speech, and vision-language modalities across 80+ languages.
The analysis examines academic literature and public benchmark datasets, delimiting coverage of proprietary industrial deployment constraints and production infrastructure optimizations.
The survey reports representative quantitative metrics from cited primary studies rather than conducting independent experimental evaluations or statistical meta-analyses.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt:
Despite providing a broad survey, this paper has several limitations:

- 1. Coverage Bias The survey highlights widely studied language pairs and might have missed indigenous or minority code-mixed languages.
- 2. Evolving Landscape Given the rapid pace of LLM research, some approaches and benchmarks described may soon be outdated or replaced by newer paradigms.
- 3. Evaluation Constraints While we include recent advances in speech and multimodal processing, the volume of research in these areas significantly lags behind text-based NLU, resulting in our taxonomy covering more text based NLU.
- 4. Practical deployment The survey mainly covers academic progress, leaving ethical, computational, and accessibility concerns in real-world deployment less examined.
- 5. Quantitative Reporting All quantitative claims are representative values reported in the cited primary works rather than aggregated or meta-analyzed statistics.
limitations.summary: The survey exhibits coverage bias toward widely studied language pairs while potentially omitting indigenous or minority languages, faces rapid obsolescence due to fast-evolving foundation model paradigms, covers text-based understanding more comprehensively than speech and multimodal processing due to literature availability, focuses primarily on academic progress rather than real-world industrial deployment considerations, and compiles representative findings from primary literature rather than computing aggregated statistical meta-analyses.

generalizability_gap: Large Language Models and code-switching benchmarks demonstrate limited cross-linguistic and cross-regional generalizability, showing 25% to 35% performance drops when tested across different geographic varieties of the same language pair. Furthermore, empirical resources remain heavily concentrated in English-centric bilingual pairs (over 72% of speech and 92% of social media datasets), leaving low-resource African, Dravidian, and Southeast Asian language pairs, non-Latin script transliterations, and trilingual switching settings critically underexplored.
methodological_gap: Current code-switching methodologies suffer from three fundamental shortcomings: (1) pre-training relies predominantly on monolingual corpora and synthetic code-switched data that achieves only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to model natural conversational switch points; (2) standard evaluation metrics (BLEU, Word Error Rate, perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge frameworks fail to capture discourse coherence, sociolinguistic intent, and dialectal nuances; and (3) architectural designs lack specialized script-aware and switch-point-aware mechanisms, leading to language confusion and jailbreak safety vulnerabilities under mixed-language prompts.
future_work: Developing inclusive, naturalistic conversational datasets for underrepresented and low-resource language pairs with participatory community curation and human-in-the-loop validation.
Designing next-generation multimodal architectures that jointly model text, speech, and vision with switch-point detection, phonemic grounding, and mixture-of-experts routing.

Establishing holistic, human-aligned evaluation paradigms that assess switch-point accuracy, semantic consistency, discourse coherence, and sociolinguistic appropriateness beyond rigid lexical matching.
Investigating multilingual safety alignment and ethical frameworks to mitigate jailbreaks, backdoor attacks, and cultural biases in code-switched systems.
Expanding code-switching research to trilingual discourse, non-Latin script transliteration normalization, and complex cross-lingual reasoning tasks.
